newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria faces Christmas of economic gloom.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria faces Christmas of economic gloom.

text.p: Crisis-ridden Bulgaria has hung out a few discreet strands of tinsel as a gesture to Christmas, but soaring prices mean a Western-style gift orgy is out of the question for families struggling to make ends meet.

In stores selling imported goods, Christmas decorations are on sale and festive music is playing, but customers stocking up on luxuries dodge shop assistants marking up prices as the lev slides lower.
The national currency has fallen steadily since the beginning of the year and sharply in the last two months. Even in dollar terms, prices for imported goods have soared.

Bonka Matova, manager of the Bonjour store in Sofia's Slaveikov square, said she was trying to keep prices as steady as possible. "If we update our prices it causes panic among the staff and customers," she said.
Asked whether she would bring prices back down if a fixed exchange rate regime was introduced in the New Year as expected at a less devalued lev rate, she said it was too early to say.
"We've had to raise our prices three times in the past month," said shop assistant Vanera Trencheva, selling Lego building bricks in the state department store TsUM.
"Some middle class parents have been saving all year to make their children's wish come true but I have to admit, most of our customers are the newly rich."

The store's gloomy-looking Father Christmas says Bulgarian children are asking for the same presents as children anywhere in the world. The girls want Barbie dolls, the boys want toy cars, trucks and guns.

But Barbie will be out of the reach of many parents this Christmas. TsUM sells a basic doll at 11,000 levs (about $22), while a glamorous Baywatch Barbie, a spin-off from the television series complete with plastic shark, is 26,500 levs.
This compares with an average monthly wage of just over 14,300 levs and an average pension of 5,700 levs. Inflation is forecast to reach about 280 percent by the end of the year.
Central heating for a small apartment costs about 7,000 levs a month and many people have switched it off.
Bulgarians complain that under communist rule they had money but there was nothing in the shops, while now, the shops are full but only the lucky few can afford to buy anything.
"Have the Bulgarian people reached the bottom yet?" runs one current joke. "Yes, but they're digging deeper."
Many of those able to afford TsUM's Barbies and Game Boys this Christmas are linked to powerful business interests who have divided much of the economy between them.
Gangland-style contract killings and car bombs are common and residents of Sofia's wealthy Lozenets district complain gunfire keeps them awake at night.
Traditionally, New Year rather than Christmas is the main holiday in the small Balkan state of 8.4 million people.
In the early 1950s, Bulgarians faced prosecution for religious observance, but by the 1980s Christmas was being celebrated quietly within families.

With the end of one-party rule, Bulgarians were officially allowed to celebrate Christmas for the first time and in 1989, Christmas mass was broadcast live on national television, offering viewers the novel sight of Communist party leaders clutching candles in the Alexander Nevsky cathedral.

"Everyone's frustrated by the high prices this year," said Dimitar Kostov, shopping for a present for his two-year-old nephew. "We're trying to find something that looks good but isn't too expensive."
The government has put its faith in a currency board regime proposed by the International Monetary Fund as a last resort after Bulgaria failed to meet targets for previous programmes.
Economists warn it will only work if it is strictly adhered to and accompanied by structural reforms, and see a tough winter ahead.
